hero.name: Kavita
hero.who: a 37-year-old new head nurse in Nashik who avoids giving honest feedback

story.b: Three months ago, Kavita became head nurse of the women's ward at a district hospital in Nashik. Before that, she was everyone's friendly didi, the one who covered shifts and shared her tiffin. Now she sees problems she does not know how to raise. Pooja, a young nurse, leaves gaps in the medication chart when she rushes. Meena, who is excellent with IV lines, is sharp with patients' families. Kavita says nothing. She fixes the charts herself after her shift and gets home at nine. Then, one bad Monday, she snaps at the whole team during handover. Feeling guilty, she brings vada pav for everyone the next day. Nobody knows what she actually expects.

ask.q: Kavita swings between silence and snapping. What does her team actually need from her?
o: Honest, direct feedback from someone who clearly cares about them
More treats and kindness, so the ward stays friendly
Strict rules and public warnings, so standards go up
ask.why: Treats without honesty let problems grow, and public warnings without care break trust. Her team needs both together: a leader who cares about them as people and still tells them clearly when the work is not good enough.

chapters.take: Real kindness at work means caring and still telling the truth.

story.b: After the evening shift, Kavita asks Pooja to join her for chai in the hospital canteen. First she asks how Pooja is managing. Pooja admits she travels two hours each way from Sinnar and is always exhausted by the end of the shift. Kavita listens. Then she opens the chart and points to two missed entries from that week. She says clearly that a gap like this could lead to a patient getting a double dose. Pooja's face goes red. Kavita does not stop there. She offers to make a simple checklist with her, and suggests Pooja fills the chart before the last hour, when she is less tired. Pooja nods, embarrassed but relieved.

ask.q: Kavita is about to talk to Pooja about the chart gaps. Which approach fits the idea best?
o: Mention it lightly as a joke, so Pooja does not feel bad
Point out the gaps firmly and leave, keeping it strictly professional
Ask how Pooja is doing, then name the gaps clearly and offer help
ask.why: A joke softens the message so much that Pooja may miss how serious it is. A firm word with no care feels like an attack. Caring about Pooja while still naming the problem clearly, with help to fix it, lets her hear it and improve.

chapters.take: Care about the person and challenge the work, both at once.

story.b: Kavita has always liked Meena. When Kavita's mother had surgery last year, Meena covered her shifts for a week without being asked. So Kavita never mentions how sharply Meena talks to worried families. It feels like loyalty. Then a patient's son complains to the medical superintendent, and a formal note goes into Meena's file. Meena comes to Kavita, hurt and confused, and asks why nobody told her earlier. Kavita has no good answer. She realises her silence was not kindness. It just let Meena walk into trouble alone. A few days later, she notices a bright new nurse, Ashok, skipping hand hygiene steps when the ward gets busy.

ask.q: Ashok is new and talented but skips hygiene steps when rushed. What should Kavita do?
o: Stay quiet for now, since he is new and might lose confidence
Tell him privately and soon, because silence could hurt him and patients
Wait for the yearly appraisal and raise it formally then
ask.why: Staying quiet feels kind, but it lets him walk into bigger trouble, as Meena did. Waiting for the appraisal turns a small fix into a formal mark. A private, early word, said with care, gives him the chance to improve while it is still easy.

chapters.take: Silence that protects feelings today can hurt people tomorrow.

story.b: One busy Monday, a patient's drip runs dry because two nurses each thought the other was watching it. Kavita feels her anger rise like milk about to boil over. She wants to shout at both of them in front of the whole ward. She remembers the bad Monday months ago, and the vada pav that fixed nothing. First she changes the drip and makes sure the patient is fine. Then she calls both nurses to the duty room. She tells them calmly what happened and why it is serious, and asks what went wrong. Together they agree on a clear spoken handover for every drip. Later, at lunch, she stops herself from complaining about them to another head nurse.

ask.q: Kavita is angry about the dry drip. Where and how should she raise it?
o: Privately with both nurses, clearly and calmly, once the patient is safe
In front of the whole ward, so everyone learns the lesson at once
Not with them at all, but with another head nurse over lunch
ask.why: Shouting in public may be honest, but it humiliates people and breaks trust. Complaining over lunch is neither caring nor direct, and it slowly poisons the team. A private, clear talk soon after keeps both the challenge and the respect.

chapters.take: Be direct without being harsh, and never talk behind backs.

story.b: Kavita realises she has started giving feedback but never asks for any. At the Friday handover, she takes a breath and asks the team one question. What is one thing I do that makes your work harder? The room goes silent. Someone studies the floor. Kavita wants to laugh and move on. Instead she counts slowly to ten in her head and waits. Finally Pooja speaks. Kavita changes the duty roster at the last minute, she says, and it ruins people's plans at home. Kavita thanks her, writes it down, and from the next week the roster goes up every Wednesday. The team notices. The next Friday, two more people speak up.

ask.q: Kavita asks her team for criticism and the room goes quiet. What should she do?
o: Move on quickly to spare everyone the awkward moment
Wait through the silence, then thank whoever speaks and act on it
Answer the question herself by listing her own small faults
ask.why: The silence is people deciding whether it is safe to speak. Moving on tells them it was not a real question, and answering herself fills the space they needed. Waiting, thanking and then visibly acting shows that speaking up is worth the risk.

chapters.take: Ask for feedback first, wait through the silence, and act on what you hear.

story.b: Pooja's charts are now neat and complete. Kavita used to say good job and move on. This time she is specific. She tells Pooja that her six o'clock chart had every dose timed and signed, and that is exactly how she caught yesterday's double entry. Pooja smiles for the rest of the shift. Kavita also starts asking each nurse what they want from their career. Pooja wants to train for the ICU, so Kavita helps her apply. Meena surprises her. She does not want a promotion. She wants to stay on the ward and be the best at difficult IV lines. Kavita had always assumed everyone wanted to move up.

ask.q: Meena says she does not want a promotion, just to stay great on the ward. How should Kavita respond?
o: Push her to apply for promotion anyway, since growth means moving up
Assume she lacks ambition and give the best chances to others
Value her choice and help her grow mastery, like training juniors
ask.why: Not everyone wants to climb. Pushing Meena upward ignores what she wants, and writing her off loses a strong nurse. People who want stability and mastery are valuable too, and a way to grow inside her role keeps her engaged.

chapters.take: Praise exactly what worked, and help each person grow their own way.

story.b: A few months later, the evening handover on the women's ward takes fifteen calm minutes. Kavita leaves by half past seven most days. Pooja has started her ICU training and tells a friend that Kavita was the first senior who ever told her the truth kindly. Meena runs a Saturday practice session on IV lines for new nurses, and complaints from families have dropped. Ashok never skips a hygiene step now. Kavita still feels nervous before a hard conversation, but she has it early, in private, often over chai. Last Friday the team told her the new roster works well and that she still interrupts during handover. She laughed, and wrote it down.

chapters.take: Care enough to say it, and say it so they can hear it.
